name: Trebbiano

lines.s10: Trebbiano is central Italy's everyday white: light, crisp and lemony, and in France, as Ugni Blanc, it is distilled into Cognac.
lines.s20: Trebbiano is a family of white grapes that share a name across central Italy, and the one that travelled is Trebbiano Toscano. It makes a light, dry white of lemon and green apple, crisp and quiet, made to be poured cold and young.
lines.s45: Trebbiano is a family name more than a single grape, shared by several different white vines of central Italy. The one that travelled is Trebbiano Toscano, which the French call Ugni Blanc. It tastes of lemon and green apple, with a faint note of almond. It is light, dry and crisp, with high acidity. It is made in steel and sold young, and in France the same sharp wine is distilled into Cognac. It is happy beside fried fish, antipasti or a simple pasta, as long as it is cold. Around Modena, the cooked juice of Trebbiano is aged for years in small casks to become traditional balsamic vinegar.
lines.sale: Trebbiano is the cold, crisp white an Italian trattoria puts on the table without being asked, and it gets on with every plate. I would pour it for the table that wants one easy white from the fried starters through to the pasta.

glass.lead: Lemon and green apple with a faint note of almond, light, dry and crisp, quiet in scent and short on the finish.

ladder.where: The Charente and Gascony, on France's Atlantic side
Central Italy, from Tuscany and Umbria to Abruzzo

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol low to moderate, body light, with little scent and a short, clean finish.

home.home: Central Italy. Trebbiano Toscano fills out Orvieto, where it is called Procanico, has a part in Frascati, and is dried with Malvasia for Vin Santo. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be Trebbiano Abruzzese, a separate vine that can age, or Toscano. Romagna and Spoleto have Trebbianos of their own. Most is made in steel and sold young.
home.abroad: As Ugni Blanc it crossed into France, where it is distilled for Cognac and Armagnac and blended into the crisp whites of Gascony, with a part in the whites of Provence. Elsewhere it is little seen on a label.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; an old vine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo a little warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a small glass for Vin Santo.
service.decant: No. A light, fresh white is poured cold, straight from the bottle.
service.age: Within a year or two as a rule; the rare old vine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo can keep twenty years.

with.dish: Antipasti: olives, cured meats, fresh cheese
with.why: a quiet wine suits a mixed plate
lemon and salt, with nothing in the way
a light body and bright acidity
the Tuscan custom at the end of dinner

labels.means: The French name of Trebbiano Toscano: the grape of Cognac and Armagnac, and of Gascony's crisp whites.
The white of Abruzzo, from Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent together.
The local name of Trebbiano Toscano in Orvieto and around Lake Bolsena.
A separate vine of Spoleto and Montefalco in Umbria: late ripening, high in acidity, with lemon peel and salt.
Old names of Verdicchio, no Trebbiano at all; Lugana's grape is now called Turbiana.

guest.q: Is Trebbiano the same as Pinot Grigio?
guest.a: No, though it fills the same place at the table. Both are light, dry and easy. Trebbiano is sharper and more lemony, where Pinot Grigio is softer, with pear.

guest.q: Is it true that Cognac is made from this grape?
guest.a: Yes. As Ugni Blanc, Trebbiano Toscano makes a thin, sharp wine low in alcohol, which is poor to drink and ideal to distil. Cognac and Armagnac both depend on it.

guest.q: Why does one Trebbiano d'Abruzzo taste plain and another so rich?
guest.a: Two vines share the name. Much is light and lemony, made for seafood. From old vines and low crops, Trebbiano Abruzzese turns waxy and salty, with hazelnut, and can keep twenty years.

compare.tell: Pinot Grigio is as light but softer, with pear and lower acidity; Trebbiano is sharper and more lemony, with a shorter finish.
Verdicchio has more flavour and a firm bitter almond finish; Trebbiano Toscano is lighter and plainer. The Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana of old labels are Verdicchio.
Garganega, as Soave, has more to say, with white peach and a bitter almond finish; Trebbiano is plainer, with lemon and green apple alone.

profile.st: Pale lemon · Body light · Acid high · Alcohol low to moderate · Dry and neutral; amber and sweet as Vin Santo
profile.fruit: Lemon, green apple and pear, faint in scent; sharper and thinner from France's Atlantic side
profile.other: A faint bitter almond; sea salt and wet stone from the better sites; hazelnut and a waxy feel in old vine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo; almost never new oak
profile.tell: Pale, light and high in acidity with very little scent: lemon, green apple and a short, clean finish, the quiet white of central Italy
profile.regions: Tuscany, Umbria, Lazio, Abruzzo and Romagna in Italy; as Ugni Blanc, Cognac, Armagnac, Gascony and Provence in France
profile.confuse: Pinot Grigio is softer, with pear; Garganega adds white peach and bitter almond; Verdicchio has more flavour and a firmer finish; Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana are Verdicchio

cards.front: Trebbiano Toscano: what do the French call it, and what for?
cards.back: Ugni Blanc. Its thin, sharp wine, low in alcohol, is distilled for Cognac and Armagnac, and it goes into the crisp whites of Gascony and of Provence.

cards.front: Why is Trebbiano called a family and not a grape?
cards.back: Several different vines share the name: Trebbiano Toscano, Abruzzese, Romagnolo and Spoletino are separate varieties. Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana are no Trebbiano at all, but Verdicchio.

cards.front: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo: which Trebbiano is in the bottle?
cards.back: Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent together. Abruzzese is a separate vine: from old vines and low crops it gives a waxy, salty white that can age.

questions.q: A guest reads the back label of an Orvieto and asks which grape Procanico is. What do you tell him?
questions.exp: Procanico is Trebbiano Toscano as Orvieto and Lake Bolsena call it, and it gives the blend crisp volume. Grechetto is its partner there, a separate grape that brings the nut and the bitter twist.

questions.q: A blind white is pale, light and dry, with high acidity, faint lemon and green apple, almost no scent, no oak and a short, clean finish. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Very little scent, high acidity and a short finish point to Trebbiano. Verdicchio would show more flavour and a firm bitter almond finish, Garganega white peach, and Fiano a waxy weight.

questions.q: A guest orders almond biscuits to finish and asks for the Tuscan wine made to go with them, from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Vin Santo is Tuscany's wine of dried Trebbiano and Malvasia, aged for years in small sealed casks and poured with almond biscuits. Recioto di Soave is dried Garganega, from the Veneto.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: central Italy, with France (as Ugni Blanc) given as abroad. Kind family: the entry describes Trebbiano Toscano, the vine a guest meets most, and names Abruzzese, Romagnolo and Spoletino as the separate vines they are.

notIn holds trebbiano di soave and trebbiano di lugana: both are Verdicchio, whose own page carries Trebbiano di Soave and Turbiana as aliases, so their questions belong to that drill and not to this one.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the nine targets are Tuscany, Umbria, Abruzzo, Lazio, Emilia-Romagna, Italy and France (whose records already name a Trebbiano or Ugni Blanc), with South West France and Provence, whose records name Ugni Blanc in Gascony and at Cassis.
Say: the Codex holds treb-BYAH-noh in the Tuscany record and treb-bee-AH-noh in the Italy, Umbria and Abruzzo records. The entry takes the first, nearer the Italian, and adds the French name.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Codex already holds Trebbiano Toscano as neutral and high in acid and as Ugni Blanc in France; Procanico in Orvieto and at Montefiascone; its part in Frascati; Vin Santo from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia with almond biscuits; Trebbiano d'Abruzzo from Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano at 85 per cent together, light and lemony as a rule and waxy, saline and nutty from old vines, living twenty years; Trebbiano Romagnolo; Trebbiano Spoletino as a separate, late ripening vine; Cognac and Armagnac from Ugni Blanc, its base wine thin, sharp and low in alcohol; Gascony and Cassis.
A doubt on a Codex record, for the owner: the France record calls Ugni Blanc the most planted white grape of France. That is a planting rank and so volatile; the entry does not repeat it.

A second doubt, for the owner: the Italy record says Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a different grape from Trebbiano Toscano, while the Abruzzo record rightly says the wine of that name may be made from either vine. Sources read add that the rules of Trebbiano d'Abruzzo also admit Bombino Bianco within the 85 per cent; the entry keeps to the Abruzzo record's wording and leaves Bombino Bianco out.

Family and not one grape: a study in the journal Vitis found most vines called Trebbiano to lack a common ancestor, with Trebbiano di Soave identical to Verdicchio and Trebbiano di Lugana very close to it. The entry therefore says several different vines and not unrelated ones, since the same work notes a tie between Abruzzese and Spoletino.

Balsamic vinegar: the consortium's own specification lists Trebbiano among the grapes whose cooked must alone makes the traditional vinegar of Modena, aged in a series of casks. The spoken line says aged for years in small casks and gives no figure.
Ugni Blanc in Cognac stands on the regional body's own page: of Tuscan origin, planted widely after phylloxera, high in acid and low in alcohol.

The ladder is a taster's reading on two rungs: at its cool limit on France's Atlantic side the wine is thin and sharp, which is why it is distilled, and central Italy gives a riper, rounder wine. Sea salt, wet stone and hazelnut are the notes the Codex gives the better Abruzzo and Umbria wines.

Left out for want of a second source or by the house rules: the white grapes once allowed in Chianti Classico and the 2006 vintage that ended it (one reference and one writer's page), the grape's role in other countries, any planting rank, the estates of Abruzzo, the origin of the name and the crossings bred from Ugni Blanc.

No dish from the Creole table is given: the oysters, the redfish, the shrimp remoulade and the crawfish are already with the neighbours of this chunk, and nothing else on that table suits so light a wine.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
